summary: Specifies how the Advanced Encryption Standard (AES) can be used as an encryption algorithm in the User-based Security Model of SNMPv3. This gives network management messages a stronger privacy option than the older DES-based choice.

eli5.summary: Messages between network managers and devices can be locked in a strong code box. This document says how to use a modern, strong lock for them.

questions: how is the iv built in snmp usm aes
subtitle: How SNMPv3 management messages get a stronger privacy option using AES in 128-bit cipher feedback mode.

tldr.problem: The User-based Security Model of SNMPv3 originally offered only CBC-DES as its privacy (encryption) protocol, and the model allows other protocols to be added.
tldr.mechanism: RFC 3826 adds the CFB128-AES-128 privacy protocol: the scopedPDU is encrypted with AES in cipher feedback mode with a 128-bit key, using an IV built from the engine's boot count, engine time and a 64-bit salt sent in the message.
tldr.outcome: It is an alternative privacy protocol that plugs into USM like the existing ones, and it must be paired with an authentication protocol because CFB mode does not detect modified ciphertext.

today: RFC 3826 is a Proposed Standard and the metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it. It remains the definition of the CFB128-AES-128 privacy protocol for the SNMP User-based Security Model, which is specified in RFC 3414.

sections.title: Adding AES to the User-based Security Model
sections.content:
The User-based Security Model (USM) is the security subsystem of SNMPv3 (RFC 3414). That RFC describes HMAC-MD5-96 and HMAC-SHA-96 as the initial authentication protocols and CBC-DES as the initial privacy protocol. USM allows other protocols to be used instead of, or alongside, these.

This memo describes CFB128-AES-128 as an alternative privacy protocol. Its main goal is a new privacy protocol based on the Advanced Encryption Standard (AES). Its major constraint is complete interchangeability with the authentication and privacy protocols already defined in USM. For a given user, the AES protocol MUST be used with one of the RFC 3414 authentication protocols or an algorithm providing equivalent functionality.
sections.eli5: SNMP already had one lock for its private messages. This document adds a newer, stronger lock that fits the same door, so devices can swap one for the other.

sections.title: The AES Cipher Parameters
sections.content:
The protocol uses AES, which NIST selected in a four-year competitive process as the replacement for DES. It runs in Cipher Feedback (CFB) mode, one of five confidentiality modes recommended by NIST Special Publication 800-38A (ECB, CBC, CFB, OFB and CTR), with the parameter S (the number of bits fed back) set to 128.

  • Key size: 128 bits.
  • Block size: 128 bits.
  • Rounds: 10.

CFB mode needs an initialization vector (IV) that is the same size as the cipher's block size. No padding is required, because the last block may have fewer than 128 bits.
sections.eli5: The lock works on the message in pieces of the same size. The last piece can be smaller, and the lock does not need any filler to make it fit.

sections.title: The Key and the Initialization Vector
sections.content:
The protocol MUST be used with an authentication protocol that generates a localized key (Kul) of at least 128 bits; the RFC 3414 protocols satisfy this. The first 128 bits of the localized key are the AES encryption key.

The 128-bit IV is the concatenation of three values, each sent most significant byte first:

  • the authoritative engine's 32-bit snmpEngineBoots (first 4 octets),
  • the engine's 32-bit snmpEngineTime (next 4 octets),
  • a local 64-bit integer (last 8 octets), initialized to a pseudo-random value at boot time.

The 64-bit integer, called the salt, is placed in the msgPrivacyParameters field as an OCTET STRING of length 8 octets, so the receiver can rebuild the same IV. The RFC recommends incrementing it by one for each message until it wraps, but any method is allowed as long as it never generates a duplicate IV for the same key. The user's secret key must be at least 128 bits (16 octets), and the keys passed to the encrypt and decrypt services MUST be 16 octets.
sections.eli5: Every message gets its own one-time twist made from a counter, a clock and a random number. The twist travels with the message so the other side can undo it.

sections.title: Encrypting and Decrypting the Data
sections.content:
The part of the message that USM encrypts is the scopedPDU. The plaintext is split into 128-bit blocks. The forward cipher operation is applied to the IV to give the first output block, and the first plaintext block is exclusive-ORed with it to give the first ciphertext block. That ciphertext block becomes the input to the next cipher operation, and so on. The last, possibly shorter, segment of r bits is exclusive-ORed with the r most significant bits of the last output block.

Decryption uses the same forward cipher function: the IV is the first input block, each ciphertext block feeds the next input block, and exclusive-OR with the output blocks recovers the plaintext.
sections.eli5: Each scrambled piece helps scramble the next one, like a chain. The receiver follows the same chain backwards to read the message.

sections.title: Processing Outgoing and Incoming Messages
sections.content:
To send, the engine builds the AES key and sets privParameters to the serialized OCTET STRING of the 64-bit integer, encrypts the scopedPDU, and serializes the result as an OCTET STRING. It returns the encrypted data, the privParameters and a success status.

To receive, the engine first checks that privParameters is an 8-octet OCTET STRING; if not, it returns a decryptionError. It extracts the 64-bit integer, builds the key and IV, and decrypts. If the data cannot be decrypted, it again returns decryptionError; otherwise it returns the decrypted scopedPDU with a success status.

The RFC also defines the abstract encryptData and decryptData service primitives that USM calls, and a small MIB module that registers the protocol identity usmAesCfb128Protocol.
sections.eli5: The sender locks the note and attaches the twist. The receiver checks the twist looks right, then unlocks the note, and complains if it cannot.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
Key guessing is described as a more probable threat than attacks on the cipher itself. The RFC recommends that passwords be at least 12 octets, that password sharing be prohibited, and that implementations support randomly generated passwords. A user's password or non-localized key MUST NOT be stored on a managed device; the localized key is stored, if at all, so one compromised device does not compromise others.

CFB security depends on a unique IV for every message encrypted with the same key. If an IV repeats, an attacker can recover the corresponding plaintext. A duplicate could occur if multiple managers talking to one authoritative engine accidentally pick the same 64-bit integer within a second, which the RFC calls very unlikely.

CFB mode does not detect ciphertext modification, so this privacy protocol MUST be used with an RFC 3414 authentication protocol or one with equivalent functionality, including integrity.
sections.eli5: A strong lock still fails if the key is easy to guess or if the same twist is used twice. And since the lock cannot tell if someone tampered with the note, a separate tamper seal is required.

sections.title: IANA Assignments
sections.content: IANA assigned OID 20 for the snmpUsmAesMIB module under the snmpModules subtree, and OID 4 for usmAesCfb128Protocol under the snmpPrivProtocols registration point defined in RFC 3411.
sections.eli5: The new lock was given its own official number so that everyone can name it the same way.

fields.name: snmpEngineBoots
fields.desc: The authoritative engine's boot count, most significant byte first.

fields.name: snmpEngineTime
fields.desc: The authoritative engine's time value, most significant byte first.

fields.name: Salt (64-bit integer)
fields.desc: Local integer sent in msgPrivacyParameters as 8 octets.
